title: Electric Vehicle Awareness and Perceived Adoption Barriers in Kerala
summary: In 2021 we asked 400 students and working people in Kerala what they knew about electric vehicles. Almost all of them knew the cars were on sale; fewer than four in ten knew the government would help pay for one. And asked what was holding electric cars back, they gave one answer more than any other: nowhere to charge.
opening: What holds electric cars back in Kerala? Nowhere to charge.
facts: Abhaya Gifty Thomas, Adhit Chandy George, Aiswarya K. S.
October 2026 · aggregate tables; no new fieldwork
abstract: This thesis examines awareness of electric vehicles, perceived barriers to adoption, and conditional purchase consideration among respondents to an online survey undertaken for a bachelor project in Kerala in 2021. The analysis uses the recoverable frequency tables for 400 respondents, comprising 299 students and 101 respondents classified as professionals. Its purpose is to establish what these observations imply for consumer information and charging policy while distinguishing sample descriptions from population estimates and stated intentions from realised demand.

Awareness of electric vehicle availability was reported by 370 respondents, or 92.50%, whereas 151 respondents, or 37.75%, reported awareness of government incentives. In a multiple-response question, unavailable charging stations were selected by 269 respondents, or 67.25%; limited model choice by 48.25%; high purchase prices by 45.50%; long charging times by 31.00%; and range anxiety by 26.75%. These percentages use respondents as the denominator and therefore need not sum to 100%. Among professionals, baseline willingness to consider an electric car was 38.61%. Consideration was higher under hypothetical conditions involving a price of INR 600,000, a range of 600 kilometres, or combined public and home charging provision. These comparisons describe aggregate response patterns and do not identify causal effects or individual changes in preference.

The results are interpreted through consumer choice, total ownership costs, information frictions, and the complementarity between vehicles and charging infrastructure. They support investigating clearer incentive information and targeted charging provision, but do not establish the optimal subsidy, charger density, or regional allocation of public investment. The absence of documented probability sampling, respondent records, and validated knowledge measures limits inference. The contribution is a transparent account of the available survey evidence and its implications for further policy evaluation.

question.lead: What did surveyed students and professionals in Kerala know about electric vehicles, and what held them back?
question.text: Our bachelor project surveyed 400 people in 2021: 299 students and 101 professionals. This 2026 revision reanalyses the summary tables of the original report; no new survey was carried out.

figure.caption: In the 2021 survey, 370 of 400 respondents (92.50%) said they knew electric vehicles were available; 151 (37.75%) said they knew about government incentives. Source: original report, Table 4.2.1 (p. 48). These are respondents' own answers, not a knowledge test, and not an estimate for Kerala as a whole.

finding.lead: Almost all respondents knew electric vehicles were available. Far fewer knew about government incentives, and the lack of charging stations was the barrier they named most often.
points: 370 of 400 respondents said they knew electric vehicles were available.
151 of 400 respondents said they knew about government incentives.
269 of 400 respondents named the lack of charging stations as a barrier. Each could name more than one.
39 of 101 professionals said they would consider an electric car if buying a new car. This is not the share who actually bought one.

limits.lead: An exploratory survey, read within its limits.
points: Most respondents were students, and the survey is not documented well enough to say whom it represents. Only the summary tables survive, not the individual answers. So it cannot say how common these views are across Kerala, follow how one person's answers changed, or show cause and effect.
Respondents could name more than one barrier, so those percentages do not add up to 100%.
Whether professionals would consider an electric car comes from separate hypothetical questions. The answers are not actual purchases, and they do not show what caused anyone's choice.

The results suggest trying clearer information about incentives and small pilots that bring charging closer to people. Decisions on investment or subsidies need evidence on actual use, costs, who benefits, and whether the money brings in buyers who would not have bought anyway. This survey alone cannot decide the best policy.
